claim: Chytrids (phylum Chytridiomycota) are a major fungal lineage of ecological importance.
source: The chytrids (phylum Chytridiomycota) are a major, predominantly unicellular fungal lineage of ecological importance.
evidence: This is a general statement about chytrids supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Some chytrid species are the causative agents of the global amphibian panzootic.
source: For example, some chytrid species are the causative agents of the global amphibian panzootic (Fisher and Garner, 2020) and virulent crop pests (van de Vossenberg et al., 2019), whilst others are algal parasites and saprotrophs in marine and freshwater ecosystems (Frenken et al., 2017; Grossart et al., 2019; Klawonn et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fisher and Garner, 2020.

claim: Some chytrid species are virulent crop pests.

evidence: Supported by citation to van de Vossenberg et al., 2019.

claim: Some chytrids are algal parasites and saprotrophs in marine and freshwater ecosystems.

evidence: Supported by citations to Frenken et al., 2017; Grossart et al., 2019; Klawonn et al., 2021.

claim: Chytrid zoospores contain large amounts of intracellular storage lipids that are consumed by grazing zooplankton.
source: Chytrid zoospores contain large amounts of intracellular storage lipids that are consumed by grazing zooplankton, making them responsible for a significant form of trophic upgrading in aquatic ecosystems (Kagami et al., 2017; Kagami et al., 2014; Kagami et al., 2007; Rasconi et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kagami et al., 2017; Kagami et al., 2014; Kagami et al., 2007; Rasconi et al., 2020.

claim: Chytrids are responsible for a significant form of trophic upgrading in aquatic ecosystems.
source: Chytrid zoospores contain large amounts of intracellular storage lipids that are consumed by grazing zooplankton, making them responsible for a significant form of trophic upgrading in aquatic ecosystems (Kagami et al., 2017; Kagami et al., 2014; Kagami et al., 2007; Rasconi et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kagami et al., 2017; Kagami et al., 2014; Kagami et al., 2007; Rasconi et al., 2020.

claim: Chytrids retain cellular traits from the last common ancestor of branching fungi that are now absent in hyphal fungi.
source: Chytrids are also important from an evolutionary perspective as they retain cellular traits from the last common ancestor of branching fungi (Figure 1A) that are now absent in hyphal fungi (Berbee et al., 2017; Nagy et al., 2018), as well as traits from the common ancestor of animals and fungi in the Opisthokonta (Medina et al., 2016; Prostak et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Berbee et al., 2017; Nagy et al., 2018 and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Chytrids retain traits from the common ancestor of animals and fungi in the Opisthokonta.
source: Chytrids are also important from an evolutionary perspective as they retain cellular traits from the last common ancestor of branching fungi (Figure 1A) that are now absent in hyphal fungi (Berbee et al., 2017; Nagy et al., 2018), as well as traits from the common ancestor of animals and fungi in the Opisthokonta (Medina et al., 2016; Prostak et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Medina et al., 2016; Prostak et al., 2021.

claim: Chytrids are powerful models to explore the origin and evolution of innovations in fungal cell biology and the wider eukaryotic tree of life.
source: This makes chytrids powerful models to explore the origin and evolution of innovations in fungal cell biology and the wider eukaryotic tree of life.
evidence: This is an inference based on the evolutionary position and retained ancestral traits of chytrids.

claim: Rhizoclosmatium globosum exhibits an archetypal chytrid life cycle and cell plan.
source: Rhizoclosmatium globosum exhibits an archetypal chytrid life cycle and cell plan delineated here into four discrete major stages.
evidence: Supported by Figure 1B showing the life cycle stages.

claim: The chytrid life cycle can be categorised into four distinctive contiguous life stages.
source: Any biological life cycle inherently represents a temporal progression, yet the chytrid life cycle can be categorised into four distinctive contiguous life stages (Berger et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Berger et al., 2005.

claim: Chytrid zoospores are transcriptionally and translationally inactive, with dormant ribosomes containing maternally derived mRNA.
source: Even though zoospores are metabolically active, they are transcriptionally and translationally inactive, with dormant ribosomes containing maternally derived mRNA (Medina and Buchler, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Medina and Buchler, 2020.

claim: The apophysis is a bulbous swelling between the cell body and rhizoid in some chytrid species.
source: The cell plan of the immature thallus can be divided into three parts (Figure 1B): the cell body which is ultimately destined for reproduction (zoosporogenesis), the rhizoid for attachment and feeding, and (in some chytrid species) a bulbous swelling between the cell body and rhizoid termed the 'apophysis', the function of which is currently poorly understood (Laundon and Cunliffe, 2021).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1B and citation to Laundon and Cunliffe, 2021.

claim: The function of the apophysis is currently poorly understood.
source: The cell plan of the immature thallus can be divided into three parts (Figure 1B): the cell body which is ultimately destined for reproduction (zoosporogenesis), the rhizoid for attachment and feeding, and (in some chytrid species) a bulbous swelling between the cell body and rhizoid termed the 'apophysis', the function of which is currently poorly understood (Laundon and Cunliffe, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Laundon and Cunliffe, 2021.

claim: Rhizoclosmatium globosum JEL800 has emerged as a promising model organism in laboratory investigations.
source: Rhizoclosmatium globosum is a widespread aquatic saprotroph and the strain R. globosum JEL800 has emerged as a promising model organism in laboratory investigations (Laundon et al., 2020; Roberts et al., 2020; Venard et al., 2020) due to an available genome (Mondo et al., 2017), easy axenic culture, and amenability to live-cell fluorescent microscopy (Laundon et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Laundon et al., 2020; Roberts et al., 2020; Venard et al., 2020; Mondo et al., 2017.

claim: R. globosum JEL800 has an available genome.

evidence: Supported by citation to Mondo et al., 2017.

claim: The volumetric transition from zoospore to germling to immature thallus exceeds an order of magnitude.
source: The orientation, subcellular localisation, and morphology of the cellular ultrastructure determined with SBF-SEM of the R. globosum zoospore, germling, and immature thallus life stages are shown in Figure 2A; Video 1; Figure 2—figure supplements 1–5, with the volumetric transition from zoospore (20.7 ± 1.7 µm3, mean ± SD) to germling (33.0 ± 2.0 µm3) to immature thallus (1116.3 ± 206.2 µm3) exceeding an order of magnitude.
evidence: Supported by volumetric measurements from SBF-SEM data shown in Figure 2A and supplementary figures.

claim: The zoospore cell body is volumetrically dominated by a structurally distinct ribosome cluster (20.5% ± 2.8 %).
source: The zoospore cell body is a prolate spheroid with a posterior flagellum and is volumetrically dominated by a structurally distinct ribosome cluster (20.5% ± 2.8 %) in the cell interior which was not detected in the other life stages (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: Supported by volumetric quantification from SBF-SEM data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: The ribosome cluster was not detected in germling and immature thallus life stages.
source: The zoospore cell body is a prolate spheroid with a posterior flagellum and is volumetrically dominated by a structurally distinct ribosome cluster (20.5% ± 2.8 %) in the cell interior which was not detected in the other life stages (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: Supported by SBF-SEM data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: There was no observed significant molecular signature associated with elevated protein synthesis in zoospores.
source: There was no observed significant molecular signature associated with elevated protein synthesis in zoospores, and relative to the mRNA present in the zoospore life stage, the germling transcriptome showed a downregulation of ribosome and ribosome biogenesis KEGG categories (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by transcriptome analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Relative to the mRNA present in the zoospore life stage, the germling transcriptome showed a downregulation of ribosome and ribosome biogenesis KEGG categories.
source: There was no observed significant molecular signature associated with elevated protein synthesis in zoospores, and relative to the mRNA present in the zoospore life stage, the germling transcriptome showed a downregulation of ribosome and ribosome biogenesis KEGG categories (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by transcriptome analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: KEGG categories linked to peroxisomes and ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters were downregulated in germlings relative to the mRNA present in zoospores.
source: Only two other KEGG categories were downregulated in germlings relative to the mRNA present in zoospores. These were linked to peroxisomes and ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters (Figure 3C), both of which are associated with lipid metabolism (discussed further below).
evidence: Supported by transcriptome analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Peroxisomes and ABC transporters are associated with lipid metabolism.
source: Only two other KEGG categories were downregulated in germlings relative to the mRNA present in zoospores. These were linked to peroxisomes and ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters (Figure 3C), both of which are associated with lipid metabolism (discussed further below).
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge about the function of peroxisomes and ABC transporters.

claim: The germling stage marks the origin of a complete cell wall, Golgi apparatuses, and peripheral bodies.
source: Following encystment, the germling stage marks the origin of a complete cell wall, Golgi apparatuses (three out of five replicates), and peripheral bodies, that is, vesicular structures bound to the cell periphery putatively associated with cell wall deposition (Figure 2A, C; Figure 2—figure supplement 2), as well as the beginning of rhizoid growth from a posterior germ tube.
evidence: Supported by SBF-SEM data shown in Figure 2A, C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Peripheral bodies are vesicular structures bound to the cell periphery putatively associated with cell wall deposition.
source: Following encystment, the germling stage marks the origin of a complete cell wall, Golgi apparatuses (three out of five replicates), and peripheral bodies, that is, vesicular structures bound to the cell periphery putatively associated with cell wall deposition (Figure 2A, C; Figure 2—figure supplement 2), as well as the beginning of rhizoid growth from a posterior germ tube.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the function of peripheral bodies based on their location and the context of cell wall formation.

claim: The germling exhibits upregulation of primary and secondary metabolism, feeding and energy release, and activation of transcription and translation KEGG categories.
source: Transcriptome analysis indicated that the germling exhibits a greater range of active processes compared to the zoospore, with upregulation of primary and secondary metabolism (e.g. amino acid and secondary metabolite biosynthesis), feeding and energy release (e.g. carbon metabolism and tricarboxylic acid cycle), and the activation of transcription and translation (e.g. spliceosome and aminoacyl-tRNA biosynthesis) KEGG categories (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by transcriptome analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: In the germling stage, there is upregulation of genes associated with proteasome activity.
source: In the germling stage, we also show upregulation of genes associated with proteasome activity (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by transcriptome analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The transition from zoospore to germling is characterized by the activation of diverse biological processes including central metabolic pathways, cellular anabolism, and feeding.
source: Taken together, these data characterise the transition from zoospore to germling with the activation of diverse biological processes including central metabolic pathways, cellular anabolism, and feeding.
evidence: This is an inference based on the transcriptome data showing upregulation of various metabolic and biosynthetic pathways.

claim: Immature thalli devoted a smaller volumetric proportion to the cell wall (IT 2.4% ± 0.3% vs. G 7.6% ± 1.2%, p < 0.01) compared to germlings.

evidence: Supported by volumetric quantification from SBF-SEM data shown in Figure 2A, D and Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: Immature thalli displayed larger glycogen stores (IT 9.4% ± 2.0% vs. G 1.3% ± 0.4%, p < 0.01) than germlings.

evidence: Supported by volumetric quantification from SBF-SEM data shown in Figure 2A, D and Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

evidence: Supported by volumetric quantification from SBF-SEM data shown in Figure 2A, D and Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: The immature thalli transcriptomes showed the upregulation of KEGG categories including endocytosis and phagosomes relative to germlings.
source: The immature thalli transcriptomes showed the upregulation of KEGG categories including endocytosis and phagosomes relative to germlings (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by transcriptome analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Immature thalli are associated with higher cytoskeletal activity compared to germlings.

claim: Some immature thallus replicates were multinucleate (1.8 ± 1.3 nuclei per cell), indicating the onset of nuclear division.
source: Some immature thallus replicates were multinucleate (1.8 ± 1.3 nuclei per cell), indicating the onset of nuclear division (Figure 2A), which is supported by the upregulation of cell cycle and DNA replication KEGG categories relative to germlings.
evidence: Supported by SBF-SEM observations shown in Figure 2A and transcriptome data.

claim: The onset of nuclear division in immature thalli is supported by the upregulation of cell cycle and DNA replication KEGG categories relative to germlings.

claim: The apophysis (12.2 ± 6.0 µm3) was observed at the immature thallus stage.
source: The apophysis (12.2 ± 6.0 µm3) was observed at the immature thallus stage (discussed further below).

claim: The biological shift from germling to immature thallus is characterized by a transition from initiating general metabolic activity to intracellular trafficking and the start of zoosporogenesis.
source: Overall, these data characterise the biological shift from germling to immature thallus, a transition from initiating general metabolic activity to intracellular trafficking and the start of zoosporogenesis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined cellular and molecular data.

claim: Precursory cell wall material is produced by zoospores at the posterior pole near the flagellum base.
source: Single-cell fluorescent labelling of chitin (the primary wall component) however showed that precursory material is produced by zoospores at the posterior pole near the flagellum base (Figure 4A) suggesting that cell wall production is initiated to some extent during the free-swimming zoospore stage of the R. globosum life cycle.
evidence: Supported by fluorescent labelling data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Cell wall production is initiated to some extent during the free-swimming zoospore stage of the R. globosum life cycle.

evidence: This is an inference based on the detection of precursory cell wall material in zoospores.

claim: There was no clear pattern of differential abundance of mRNA sequences of putative chitin synthase genes between the life stages overall.
source: There was no clear pattern of differential abundance of mRNA sequences of these genes between the life stages overall, however mRNA from five putative chitin synthase genes were abundant during the zoospore stage (Figure 4A; Supplementary file 4 Source Data).
evidence: Supported by transcriptome analysis shown in Figure 4A and Supplementary file 4.

claim: mRNA from five putative chitin synthase genes were abundant during the zoospore stage.

claim: Cell wall formation is a dynamic process throughout the chytrid life cycle, with alternative synthesis enzymes employed at different stages.
source: Together, this suggests that cell wall formation is a dynamic process throughout the chytrid life cycle, with alternative synthesis enzymes employed at different stages.

claim: R. globosum zoospores and germlings possess the archetypal single lipid globule (Z 0.9 ± 0.6 and G 1.9 ± 1.1 µm3).
source: Fluorescent labelling and SBF-SEM reconstructions showed that R. globosum zoospores and germlings possess the archetypal single lipid globule (Z 0.9 ± 0.6 and G 1.9 ± 1.1 µm3) whereas immature thalli have multiple (68.8 ± 55.2) but smaller (0.5 ± 0.8 µm3) globules scattered throughout the cell body (Figure 4A–B; Video 2).
evidence: Supported by fluorescent labelling and SBF-SEM data shown in Figure 4A-B and Video 2.

claim: Immature thalli have multiple (68.8 ± 55.2) but smaller (0.5 ± 0.8 µm3) lipid globules scattered throughout the cell body.

evidence: Supported by fluorescent labelling and SBF-SEM data shown in Figure 4A-B and Video 2.

claim: The lipid globule in the zoospore and germling stages was associated with a posteriorly oriented structure called the rumposome and an anteriorly oriented microbody that likely functions as a lipid-processing peroxisome.
source: The lipid globule (red) in the zoospore and germling stages was associated with a posteriorly oriented structure called the rumposome (grey), which is a chytrid-specific organelle putatively associated with cell signalling (Powell, 1983), and an anteriorly oriented microbody (pink) that likely functions as a lipid-processing peroxisome (Powell, 1976; Figure 4B–C; Video 2).
evidence: Supported by SBF-SEM data shown in Figure 4B-C and Video 2, and citations to Powell, 1983 and Powell, 1976.

claim: The rumposome is a chytrid-specific organelle putatively associated with cell signalling.

evidence: Supported by citation to Powell, 1983.

claim: The rumposome was larger in zoospores than in germlings (Z 0.3% ± 0.0% vs. G 0.1% ± 0.1%, p < 0.001).

claim: The larger rumposome in zoospores indicates increased activity in zoospores.

evidence: This is an inference based on the size difference of the rumposome between life stages.

claim: Glycolipids were present in both zoospores (40.7% ± 27.1%) and immature thalli (40.6% ± 27.3%), but below detection in germlings.
source: Likewise, glycolipids were present in both zoospores (40.7% ± 27.1%) and immature thalli (40.6% ± 27.3%), but below detection in germlings.
evidence: Supported by lipid analysis data.

claim: Polar lipids were below detection in zoospores yet present in germlings (51.7% ± 27.5%) and immature thalli (74.0% ± 3.4%).
source: Conversely, polar lipids were below detection in zoospores yet present in germlings (51.7% ± 27.5%) and immature thalli (74.0% ± 3.4%).
evidence: Supported by lipid analysis data.

claim: Zoospores contain increased abundance of mRNA of genes in KEGG categories associated with peroxisome activity and ABC transporters compared to germlings.
source: Comparison of the zoospore and germling transcriptomes suggest that the zoospores contain increased abundance of mRNA of genes in KEGG categories associated with peroxisome activity and ABC transporters (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by transcriptome analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Most of the genes identified under the peroxisome category are putatively involved in lipid oxidation and acyl-CoA metabolism.
source: Most of the genes identified under the peroxisome category are putatively involved in lipid oxidation and acyl-CoA metabolism (Figure 3C; Figure 3—source data 1), and therefore likely involved in the catabolic processing of the lipid globule.
evidence: Supported by analysis of genes in the peroxisome category shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—source data 1.

claim: Peroxisome genes are likely involved in the catabolic processing of the lipid globule.
source: Most of the genes identified under the peroxisome category are putatively involved in lipid oxidation and acyl-CoA metabolism (Figure 3C; Figure 3—source data 1), and therefore likely involved in the catabolic processing of the lipid globule.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known function of peroxisome genes and their upregulation in zoospores.

claim: Lipid reductases were detected, which have previously been identified with phospholipid anabolism and suggest increased phospholipid synthesis for membrane production.
source: Lipid reductases were also detected, which have previously been identified with phospholipid anabolism (Lodhi and Semenkovich, 2014) and suggest increased phospholipid synthesis for membrane production.
evidence: Supported by detection of lipid reductases in the transcriptome and citation to Lodhi and Semenkovich, 2014.

claim: ABC transporters are involved in lipid transport into peroxisomes from lipid stores.
source: ABC transporters are also involved in lipid transport into peroxisomes from lipid stores (Tarling et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tarling et al., 2013.

claim: Glycolipid, and potentially sphingolipid, catabolism from storage lipid utilisation from the globule, possibly via the peroxisome, and polar lipid anabolism are taking place during the transition from zoospore to germling.
source: With the quantification of lipids discussed above, these results suggest that glycolipid, and potentially sphingolipid, catabolism from storage lipid utilisation from the globule, possibly via the peroxisome, and polar lipid anabolism are taking place during the transition from zoospore to germling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined lipid quantification and transcriptome data.

claim: Genes associated with fatty acid degradation and peroxisomes were upregulated in the immature thallus stage compared to the germling stage.
source: We also observed the upregulation of genes associated with fatty acid degradation and peroxisomes in the immature thallus stage compared to the germling stage (Figure 3F) coinciding with new lipids being produced (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by transcriptome analysis shown in Figure 3F and lipid data in Figure 4.

claim: In immature thalli lipid production is driven by an interplay of fatty acid degradation and lipid anabolism.
source: This suggests that in immature thalli lipid production is driven by an interplay of fatty acid degradation and lipid anabolism, illustrating that some aspects of lipid catabolism and conversion in zoospores are bidirectionally repurposed for anabolism in immature thalli.
evidence: This is an inference based on the upregulation of both catabolic and anabolic lipid-related genes in immature thalli.

claim: Some aspects of lipid catabolism and conversion in zoospores are bidirectionally repurposed for anabolism in immature thalli.
source: This suggests that in immature thalli lipid production is driven by an interplay of fatty acid degradation and lipid anabolism, illustrating that some aspects of lipid catabolism and conversion in zoospores are bidirectionally repurposed for anabolism in immature thalli.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of some genes upregulated in both zoospores and immature thalli.

claim: The apophysis exhibits high endomembrane density and active intracellular trafficking between the feeding rhizoids and cell body.
source: The apophysis is ubiquitous across the Chytridiomycota (James et al., 2006), but the function of the structure is poorly understood (Laundon and Cunliffe, 2021). Here, we show that the apophysis exhibits high endomembrane density and active intracellular trafficking between the feeding rhizoids and cell body (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by SBF-SEM and live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Live-population imaging of FM1–43 labelled endomembrane in R. globosum cells showed stability in fluorescence at the beginning of the life cycle (0–2 hr), before a constant increase to the point of zoospore release.
source: Live-population imaging of FM1–43 labelled endomembrane in R. globosum cells (excluding apophysis and rhizoids) showed stability in fluorescence at the beginning of the life cycle (0–2 hr), before a constant increase to the point of zoospore release (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Immature thalli devoted a larger proportion of cell body volume to endomembrane than zoospores and germlings (Z 2.3% ± 1.5% vs. G 7.6% ± 0.9% vs. IT 13.0% ± 1.8%, p < 0.001).
source: Matching this, SBF-SEM reconstruction revealed that immature thalli devoted a larger proportion of cell body volume to endomembrane than zoospores and germlings (Z 2.3% ± 1.5% vs. G 7.6% ± 0.9% vs. IT 13.0% ± 1.8%, p < 0.001), as well as vacuoles (Figures 2B–D–5B; Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by volumetric quantification from SBF-SEM data shown in Figures 2B-D, 5B and Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: Apophyses displayed even greater endomembrane than their corresponding cell bodies (apophysis 12.2% ± 5.2% vs. cell body 2.7% ± 0.6%, p < 0.01).
source: The immature thalli SBF-SEM reconstructions showed that apophyses displayed even greater endomembrane than their corresponding cell bodies (apophysis 12.2% ± 5.2% vs. cell body 2.7% ± 0.6%, p < 0.01) (Figure 5C–D; Figure 5—figure supplement 1; Video 4).
evidence: Supported by volumetric quantification from SBF-SEM data shown in Figure 5C-D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Video 4.

claim: Apophyses had comparatively more cell wall than the larger cell bodies (A 11.0% ± 0.5% vs. CB 2.4% ± 0.3%, p < 0.01).
source: Apophyses also had comparatively more cell wall than the larger cell bodies (A 11.0% ± 0.5% vs. CB 2.4% ± 0.3%, p < 0.01) (Figure 5D; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by volumetric quantification from SBF-SEM data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: In R. globosum the cytoplasm between the apophysis and the cell body is connected via an annular pore (0.40 ± 0.07 µm in diameter) in a distinctive chitin-rich pseudo-septum.
source: In R. globosum the cytoplasm between the apophysis and the cell body is connected via an annular pore (0.40 ± 0.07 µm in diameter) in a distinctive chitin-rich pseudo-septum (Figure 5E, G), causing spatial division within the immature thallus cell plan.
evidence: Supported by SBF-SEM and fluorescent labelling data shown in Figure 5E, G.

claim: The annular pore in the pseudo-septum causes spatial division within the immature thallus cell plan.
source: In R. globosum the cytoplasm between the apophysis and the cell body is connected via an annular pore (0.40 ± 0.07 µm in diameter) in a distinctive chitin-rich pseudo-septum (Figure 5E, G), causing spatial division within the immature thallus cell plan.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observation of the pseudo-septum with a pore.

claim: Live single-cell imaging showed dynamic endomembrane activity in the apophysis linking the intracellular traffic between the rhizoid system and posterior base of the cell body via the pore.
source: Live single-cell imaging showed dynamic endomembrane activity in the apophysis linking the intracellular traffic between the rhizoid system and posterior base of the cell body via the pore (Video 5).
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Video 5.

claim: A function of the apophysis is to act as a cellular junction that sorts intracellular traffic and channels material from feeding rhizoids through the pseudo-septal pore to the cell body dedicated for reproduction.
source: Taken together, we propose that a function of the apophysis is to act as a cellular junction that sorts intracellular traffic and channels material from feeding rhizoids through the pseudo-septal pore to the cell body dedicated for reproduction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the high endomembrane density in the apophysis and observed trafficking through the pore.

claim: The volume of the SBF-SEM reconstructed mature zoosporangium was 3651.5 µm3.
source: The volume of the SBF-SEM reconstructed mature zoosporangium was 3651.5 µm3, showing that a single chytrid cell volumetrically increases by more than two orders of magnitude over its entire life cycle.
evidence: Supported by volumetric measurement from SBF-SEM reconstruction.

claim: A single chytrid cell volumetrically increases by more than two orders of magnitude over its entire life cycle.
source: The volume of the SBF-SEM reconstructed mature zoosporangium was 3651.5 µm3, showing that a single chytrid cell volumetrically increases by more than two orders of magnitude over its entire life cycle.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the volume of the zoospore (20.7 µm3) to the mature zoosporangium (3651.5 µm3).

claim: The developing zoospores were flagellate, with the flagellum coiled round the cell body in two neat and complete rotations.
source: The developing zoospores were flagellate, with the flagellum coiled round the cell body in two neat and complete rotations (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by SBF-SEM reconstruction shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Zoospores are held within the cell wall of the zoosporangium during zoosporogenesis, before exiting through the anteriorly oriented discharge pore when developed.
source: Zoospores are held within the cell wall of the zoosporangium during zoosporogenesis (Figure 6B), before exiting through the anteriorly oriented discharge pore (an aperture in the cell wall) when developed.
evidence: Supported by SBF-SEM reconstruction shown in Figure 6B and knowledge of chytrid biology.

claim: During development, the discharge pore is obstructed by a fibrillar discharge plug (49.7 µm3 in volume).
source: During development, the pore is obstructed by a fibrillar discharge plug (49.7 µm3 in volume) (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by SBF-SEM reconstruction shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Relative to mature free-swimming zoospores, developing zoospores in the zoosporangium displayed an amoeboid morphology.
source: Relative to mature free-swimming zoospores, developing zoospores in the zoosporangium displayed an amoeboid morphology and had greater intracellular trafficking, characterised by a larger volumetric proportion of endomembrane (DZ 1.7% ± 0.3% vs. MZ 0.9% ± 0.4%, p < 0.05), vacuoles (DZ 8.4% ± 2.1% vs. MZ 2.3% ± 1.5%, p < 0.001) and the presence of Golgi apparatuses and a vesicle class not observed in mature free-swimming zoospores (Figure 6D–E; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by SBF-SEM data shown in Figure 6D-E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Developing zoospores in the zoosporangium had greater intracellular trafficking than mature free-swimming zoospores, characterised by a larger volumetric proportion of endomembrane (DZ 1.7% ± 0.3% vs. MZ 0.9% ± 0.4%, p < 0.05).
source: Relative to mature free-swimming zoospores, developing zoospores in the zoosporangium displayed an amoeboid morphology and had greater intracellular trafficking, characterised by a larger volumetric proportion of endomembrane (DZ 1.7% ± 0.3% vs. MZ 0.9% ± 0.4%, p < 0.05), vacuoles (DZ 8.4% ± 2.1% vs. MZ 2.3% ± 1.5%, p < 0.001) and the presence of Golgi apparatuses and a vesicle class not observed in mature free-swimming zoospores (Figure 6D–E; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by volumetric quantification from SBF-SEM data shown in Figure 6D-E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Developing zoospores in the zoosporangium had a larger volumetric proportion of vacuoles (DZ 8.4% ± 2.1% vs. MZ 2.3% ± 1.5%, p < 0.001) than mature free-swimming zoospores.
source: Relative to mature free-swimming zoospores, developing zoospores in the zoosporangium displayed an amoeboid morphology and had greater intracellular trafficking, characterised by a larger volumetric proportion of endomembrane (DZ 1.7% ± 0.3% vs. MZ 0.9% ± 0.4%, p < 0.05), vacuoles (DZ 8.4% ± 2.1% vs. MZ 2.3% ± 1.5%, p < 0.001) and the presence of Golgi apparatuses and a vesicle class not observed in mature free-swimming zoospores (Figure 6D–E; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by volumetric quantification from SBF-SEM data shown in Figure 6D-E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Developing zoospores in the zoosporangium had Golgi apparatuses and a vesicle class not observed in mature free-swimming zoospores.
source: Relative to mature free-swimming zoospores, developing zoospores in the zoosporangium displayed an amoeboid morphology and had greater intracellular trafficking, characterised by a larger volumetric proportion of endomembrane (DZ 1.7% ± 0.3% vs. MZ 0.9% ± 0.4%, p < 0.05), vacuoles (DZ 8.4% ± 2.1% vs. MZ 2.3% ± 1.5%, p < 0.001) and the presence of Golgi apparatuses and a vesicle class not observed in mature free-swimming zoospores (Figure 6D–E; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by SBF-SEM data shown in Figure 6D-E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Developing zoospores in the zoosporangium exhibited larger glycogen stores (DV 5.5% ± 1.5% vs. MV 1.6% ± 1.2%, p < 0.01) than mature free-swimming zoospores.
source: Developing zoospores in the zoosporangium also exhibited larger glycogen stores (DV 5.5% ± 1.5% vs. MV 1.6% ± 1.2%, p < 0.01), indicating that glycogen utilisation occurs between the two stages, and a smaller rumposome (DV 0.1% ± 0.0% vs. MZ 1.3% ± 0.0%, p < 0.001) (Figure 6D–E) than their mature free-swimming counterparts.
evidence: Supported by volumetric quantification from SBF-SEM data shown in Figure 6D-E.

claim: Glycogen utilisation occurs between developing zoospores in the zoosporangium and mature free-swimming zoospores.
source: Developing zoospores in the zoosporangium also exhibited larger glycogen stores (DV 5.5% ± 1.5% vs. MV 1.6% ± 1.2%, p < 0.01), indicating that glycogen utilisation occurs between the two stages, and a smaller rumposome (DV 0.1% ± 0.0% vs. MZ 1.3% ± 0.0%, p < 0.001) (Figure 6D–E) than their mature free-swimming counterparts.
evidence: This is an inference based on the difference in glycogen stores between the two stages.

claim: Developing zoospores in the zoosporangium had a smaller rumposome (DV 0.1% ± 0.0% vs. MZ 1.3% ± 0.0%, p < 0.001) than mature free-swimming zoospores.
source: Developing zoospores in the zoosporangium also exhibited larger glycogen stores (DV 5.5% ± 1.5% vs. MV 1.6% ± 1.2%, p < 0.01), indicating that glycogen utilisation occurs between the two stages, and a smaller rumposome (DV 0.1% ± 0.0% vs. MZ 1.3% ± 0.0%, p < 0.001) (Figure 6D–E) than their mature free-swimming counterparts.
evidence: Supported by volumetric quantification from SBF-SEM data shown in Figure 6D-E.

claim: The amoeboid morphology of the developing zoospores was in part a result of possible endocytotic engulfment activity, where vacuoles extended from within the zoospore cell interior to the surrounding interstitial maternal cytoplasm of the zoosporangium.
source: The amoeboid morphology of the developing zoospores was in part a result of possible endocytotic engulfment activity, where vacuoles extended from within the zoospore cell interior to the surrounding interstitial maternal cytoplasm of the zoosporangium (Figure 6F–G).
evidence: Supported by SBF-SEM data shown in Figure 6F-G.

claim: Such vacuoles were found in every replicate (2.0 ± 0.7 vacuoles per replicate).
source: Such vacuoles were found in every replicate (2.0 ± 0.7 vacuoles per replicate).
evidence: Supported by quantification from SBF-SEM data.

claim: The zoospore vacuoles contained electron-dense cargo similar to lipids.
source: The zoospore vacuoles contained electron-dense cargo similar to lipids (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by SBF-SEM observations shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Endocytosis is a mode by which resources are trafficked from the maternal cytoplasm into developing zoospores post-cleavage.
source: The prominence of this proposed engulfment across replicates indicates the possibility that endocytosis is a mode by which resources are trafficked from the maternal cytoplasm into developing zoospores post-cleavage, and that zoospore development does not cease once cleavage has been completed.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observation of vacuoles extending to the maternal cytoplasm.

claim: Zoospore development does not cease once cleavage has been completed.
source: The prominence of this proposed engulfment across replicates indicates the possibility that endocytosis is a mode by which resources are trafficked from the maternal cytoplasm into developing zoospores post-cleavage, and that zoospore development does not cease once cleavage has been completed.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of continued resource uptake after cleavage.

claim: Developing zoospores did not yet display a detectable ribosomal cluster, as in the free-swimming zoospores.
source: Notably, developing zoospores did not yet display a detectable ribosomal cluster, as in the free-swimming zoospores (Figure 2), indicating that this structure is formed later in zoospore development than captured here.
evidence: Supported by SBF-SEM observations shown in Figure 2.

claim: The ribosomal cluster is formed later in zoospore development than captured in the developing zoospore stage.
source: Notably, developing zoospores did not yet display a detectable ribosomal cluster, as in the free-swimming zoospores (Figure 2), indicating that this structure is formed later in zoospore development than captured here.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of the ribosomal cluster in developing zoospores but presence in mature zoospores.

claim: The only KEGG categories higher in free-swimming zoospores than in the mature zoosporangia samples were associated with ribosomes.
source: The only KEGG categories higher in free-swimming zoospores than in the mature zoosporangia samples were associated with ribosomes (Figure 6J).
evidence: Supported by transcriptome analysis shown in Figure 6J.

claim: Ribosome clusters have been observed in zoospores throughout the Chytridiomycota and in the closely related Blastocladiomycota.
source: Historically called the 'nuclear cap', ribosome clusters have been observed in zoospores throughout the Chytridiomycota (e.g. Koch, 1961) and in the closely related Blastocladiomycota (e.g. Lovett, 1963).
evidence: Supported by citations to Koch, 1961 and Lovett, 1963.

claim: In Blastocladiella, the ribosome cluster dissipates during the transition between the free-swimming zoospore and germling stages.
source: Lovett, 1963, showed in Blastocladiella (Blastocladiomycota), as we show here with R. globosum, the ribosome cluster dissipates during the transition between the free-swimming zoospore and germling stages causing the release of the previously contained ribosomes throughout the cell.
evidence: Supported by citation to Lovett, 1963.

claim: The role of the ribosome cluster is to maintain the ribosomes through the zoospore stage and to spatially isolate the ribosomes to prevent translation occurring until the germling stage.
source: Lovett, 1968; Lovett, 1963, related the Blastocladiella zoospore ribosome cluster and subsequent dissipation with the biological activity of the cell during the zoospore-germling transition, proposing the role of the cluster was to maintain the ribosomes through the zoospore stage and to spatially isolate the ribosomes to prevent translation occurring until when the cluster dissipates (i.e. the germling stage) and protein synthesis is initiated.
evidence: Supported by citations to Lovett, 1968; Lovett, 1963.

claim: Transcription and translation are inactive in zoospores which contain maternally provisioned mRNA and dormant ribosomes.
source: Subsequent investigations into transcription and translation in chytrids and the Blastocladiomycota established that these processes are inactive in zoospores which contain maternally provisioned mRNA and dormant ribosomes (Barstow and Lovett, 1974; Jaworski, 1976; LéJohn and Lovett, 1966; Lovett, 1968; Schmoyer and Lovett, 1969; Silva et al., 1987).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barstow and Lovett, 1974; Jaworski, 1976; LéJohn and Lovett, 1966; Lovett, 1968; Schmoyer and Lovett, 1969; Silva et al., 1987.

claim: Rosenblum et al., 2008, detected high levels of transcripts associated with posttranslational protein modification in Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd) zoospores, but low transcriptional activity.
source: Similarly, Rosenblum et al., 2008, detected high levels of transcripts associated with posttranslational protein modification in Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd) zoospores, but low transcriptional activity.
evidence: Supported by citation to Rosenblum et al., 2008.

claim: The chytrid zoospore represents a sophisticated and well-adapted life stage specialised for dispersal to new growth substrates or hosts rather than general metabolism.
source: Taken together, the chytrid zoospore represents a sophisticated and well-adapted life stage specialised for dispersal to new growth substrates or hosts rather than general metabolism, which is only initiated by the release of the ribosome cluster at the germling stage once favourable conditions are found.
evidence: This is an inference based on the transcriptional inactivity and ribosome cluster characteristics of zoospores.

claim: General metabolism is only initiated by the release of the ribosome cluster at the germling stage once favourable conditions are found.
source: Taken together, the chytrid zoospore represents a sophisticated and well-adapted life stage specialised for dispersal to new growth substrates or hosts rather than general metabolism, which is only initiated by the release of the ribosome cluster at the germling stage once favourable conditions are found.
evidence: This is an inference based on the dissipation of the ribosome cluster and activation of metabolic pathways in germlings.

claim: Similar upregulation of metabolic pathways has been observed at the transcriptional level associated with conidial germination in dikaryan fungi.
source: Similar upregulation of metabolic pathways has been observed at the transcriptional level associated with conidial germination in dikaryan fungi (Sharma et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sharma et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2018.

claim: Proteasome genes are necessary for dikaryan germination.
source: Interestingly, we detected the upregulation of proteasome genes in the germling relative to the zoospore mRNA content, which are also necessary for dikaryan germination (Seong et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Seong et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2011.

claim: The internalised flagellum is disassembled and degraded in the germling stage, at least partially by proteasome-dependent proteolysis.
source: A previous study into flagellar retraction in R. globosum showed that the internalised flagellum is disassembled and degraded in the germling stage, at least partially by proteasome-dependent proteolysis (Venard et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Venard et al., 2020.

claim: Increased proteasome-associated mRNA may be associated with flagellar degradation and the recycling of redundant zoospore machinery in the germling.
source: Our finding of increased proteasome-associated mRNA may likewise be associated with flagellar degradation and the recycling of redundant zoospore machinery in the germling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the upregulation of proteasome genes and previous findings on flagellar degradation.

claim: Highly vacuolated dikaryan cells are associated with diverse cellular processes including general homeostasis, protein sorting, cell cycling, and intracellular trafficking.
source: Highly vacuolated dikaryan cells (El Ghaouth et al., 1994; Gow and Gooday, 1987) are associated with diverse cellular processes including general homeostasis, protein sorting, cell cycling, and intracellular trafficking (Veses et al., 2008), any of which could at least partially explain the high vacuolisation of immature chytrid thalli.
evidence: Supported by citations to El Ghaouth et al., 1994; Gow and Gooday, 1987; Veses et al., 2008.

claim: The role of actin in vacuolisation and endocytosis has been demonstrated in yeast.
source: The role of actin in vacuolisation and endocytosis has been demonstrated in yeast (Eitzen et al., 2002; Gachet and Hyams, 2005), similar to our observations here in R. globosum.
evidence: Supported by citations to Eitzen et al., 2002; Gachet and Hyams, 2005.

claim: Arp2/3-dependent actin dynamics drive crawling α-motility in some chytrid zoospores when moving freely in the environment.
source: Arp2/3-dependent actin dynamics drive crawling α-motility in some chytrid zoospores when moving freely in the environment (Fritz-Laylin et al., 2017; Medina et al., 2020) and the presence of animal-like actin components that have been lost in multicellular fungi makes chytrids useful models to investigate the evolution of the fungal cytoskeleton (Prostak et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fritz-Laylin et al., 2017; Medina et al., 2020.

claim: The presence of animal-like actin components that have been lost in multicellular fungi makes chytrids useful models to investigate the evolution of the fungal cytoskeleton.
source: Arp2/3-dependent actin dynamics drive crawling α-motility in some chytrid zoospores when moving freely in the environment (Fritz-Laylin et al., 2017; Medina et al., 2020) and the presence of animal-like actin components that have been lost in multicellular fungi makes chytrids useful models to investigate the evolution of the fungal cytoskeleton (Prostak et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Prostak et al., 2021.

claim: R. globosum zoospores do not crawl.
source: Although R. globosum zoospores do not crawl, the immature thallus has actin patches, cables, and perinuclear shells (Prostak et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on knowledge of R. globosum zoospore behavior.

claim: The immature thallus has actin patches, cables, and perinuclear shells.
source: Although R. globosum zoospores do not crawl, the immature thallus has actin patches, cables, and perinuclear shells (Prostak et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Prostak et al., 2021.

claim: For a non-crawling chytrid, actin-associated gene transcripts are increased in immature thalli and this life stage is associated with high vacuolisation and possible endocytosis, which together could be associated with the early onset of zoosporogenesis.
source: Here, we show that, for a non-crawling chytrid, actin-associated gene transcripts are increased in immature thalli and that this life stage is associated with high vacuolisation and possible endocytosis, which together could be associated with the early onset of zoosporogenesis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined observations of increased actin transcripts, vacuolisation, and the onset of cell cycle genes.

claim: Higher levels of putative chitin synthase gene transcripts in wall-less zoospores was coupled with the detection of precursory cell wall material at the base of the R. globosum flagellum.
source: Higher levels of putative chitin synthase gene transcripts (e.g. ORY39038) in wall-less zoospores was coupled with the detection of precursory cell wall material at the base of the R. globosum flagellum.
evidence: Supported by transcriptome data and fluorescent labelling observations.

claim: Bd transcriptomes suggest some chitin synthases to be more abundant in zoospores than in sessile thalli.
source: Bd transcriptomes also suggest some chitin synthases to be more abundant in zoospores than in sessile thalli (Rosenblum et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rosenblum et al., 2008.

claim: Chitin synthase activity has been shown to be associated with the Blastocladiella emersonii zoospore membrane.
source: Chitin synthase activity has been shown to be associated with the Blastocladiella emersonii zoospore membrane (Dalley and Sonneborn, 1982).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dalley and Sonneborn, 1982.

claim: During the B. emersonii zoospore-germling transition glycolipids decrease and phospholipids increase.
source: Similarly, during the B. emersonii zoospore-germling transition glycolipids decrease and phospholipids increase (Dalley and Sonneborn, 1982).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dalley and Sonneborn, 1982.

claim: Previous research has characterised fatty acid profiles in chytrids and shown differences between chytrid zoospores and sessile thalli of the same species.
source: Previous research has characterised fatty acid profiles in chytrids (Akinwole et al., 2014; Gerphagnon et al., 2019; Rasconi et al., 2020) and shown differences between chytrid zoospores and sessile thalli of the same species (Taube et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Akinwole et al., 2014; Gerphagnon et al., 2019; Rasconi et al., 2020; Taube et al., 2019.

claim: The Nile Red emission spectrum undergoes a red shift in increasingly polar environments.
source: As the Nile Red emission spectrum undergoes a red shift in increasingly polar environments (Bertozzini et al., 2011), we propose that our live-cell data do not quantify the structural degradation of the lipid globule per se but rather biochemical polarisation as neutral storage lipids are catabolised and polar phospholipids are synthesised.
evidence: Supported by citation to Bertozzini et al., 2011.

claim: The live-cell Nile Red data do not quantify the structural degradation of the lipid globule per se but rather biochemical polarisation as neutral storage lipids are catabolised and polar phospholipids are synthesised.
source: As the Nile Red emission spectrum undergoes a red shift in increasingly polar environments (Bertozzini et al., 2011), we propose that our live-cell data do not quantify the structural degradation of the lipid globule per se but rather biochemical polarisation as neutral storage lipids are catabolised and polar phospholipids are synthesised.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of Nile Red and the observed lipid changes.

claim: Glycogen catabolism between developing and mature free-swimming zoospores contributes to the zoospore energy budget during motility.
source: The larger volumetric proportion of glycogen stores in developing zoospores over mature free-swimming zoospores also indicates that glycogen catabolism between the two stages contributes to the zoospore energy budget during motility as previously proposed (Powell, 1979).
evidence: This is an inference based on the difference in glycogen stores and citation to Powell, 1979.

claim: The enzymatic function of LRM-associated microbodies as lipolytic organelles has been previously proposed.
source: The enzymatic function of LRM-associated microbodies as lipolytic organelles has been previously proposed (Powell, 1979; Powell, 1977; Powell, 1976), where evidence suggests that enzymatic activity increases following germination (Powell, 1976).
evidence: Supported by citations to Powell, 1979; Powell, 1977; Powell, 1976.

claim: This organelle may have bidirectional function and be associated with lipid production (anabolism and conversion) as well as catabolism.
source: From our data, this organelle may have bidirectional function and be associated with lipid production (anabolism and conversion) as well as catabolism.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the presence of the microbody in both catabolic and anabolic stages.

claim: Previous hypotheses have proposed that the rumposome is associated with environmental reception and signal transduction in flagellar regulation.
source: A key component of the LRM is the enigmatic chytrid rumposome, which was larger in zoospores than germlings. Previous hypotheses have proposed that this organelle is associated with environmental reception and signal transduction in flagellar regulation (Dorward and Powell, 1983).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dorward and Powell, 1983.

claim: An enlarged rumposome in motile zoospores would support a flagellar role, but its retention in germlings implies additional functions.
source: An enlarged rumposome in motile zoospores would support a flagellar role, but its retention in germlings implies additional functions, unless there is a prolonged delay in its degradation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the size difference and persistence of the rumposome across life stages.

claim: Comparable intravacuolar inclusions have been identified in chytrid and dikaryan fungi in the past.
source: The bulk of lipids in immature thalli during anabolism were intravacuolar and comparable intravacuolar inclusions have been identified in chytrid and dikaryan fungi in the past (Beakes et al., 1992; Bourett and Howard, 1994; Lösel, 1990).
evidence: Supported by citations to Beakes et al., 1992; Bourett and Howard, 1994; Lösel, 1990.

claim: Intravacuolar lipid droplets have been previously investigated in yeast but in a catabolic capacity.
source: Intravacuolar lipid droplets have been previously investigated in yeast but in a catabolic capacity (van Zutphen et al., 2014; Vevea et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to van Zutphen et al., 2014; Vevea et al., 2015.

claim: De novo storage lipid synthesis is associated with the ER.
source: Although de novo storage lipid synthesis is associated with the ER (Vevea et al., 2015), the vacuoles identified here may cache and aggregate nascent globules as part of the lipid anabolic pathway.
evidence: Supported by citation to Vevea et al., 2015.

claim: The vacuoles identified in immature thalli may cache and aggregate nascent globules as part of the lipid anabolic pathway.
source: Although de novo storage lipid synthesis is associated with the ER (Vevea et al., 2015), the vacuoles identified here may cache and aggregate nascent globules as part of the lipid anabolic pathway.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observation of intravacuolar lipids during anabolism.

claim: The apophysis is ubiquitous across the Chytridiomycota.
source: The function of the chytrid apophysis has long been overlooked, despite its ubiquity in the Chytridiomycota (Powell, 1974; Powell and Gillette, 1987; Taylor and Fuller, 1980).
evidence: Supported by citations to Powell, 1974; Powell and Gillette, 1987; Taylor and Fuller, 1980.

claim: The ability of multicellular dikaryan fungi to translocate assimilated nutrients through their hyphal network from the site of uptake is sophisticated.
source: The ability of multicellular dikaryan fungi to translocate assimilated nutrients through their hyphal network from the site of uptake is sophisticated (van't Padje et al., 2021; Whiteside et al., 2019), and the observed analogous endomembrane flow from feeding rhizoids to the cell body in chytrids is perhaps not surprising.
evidence: Supported by citations to van't Padje et al., 2021; Whiteside et al., 2019.

claim: The pseudo-septation of the apophysis and rhizoids from the cell body is evidence for functional compartmentation (i.e. feeding vs. reproduction) within the thallus of a unicellular fungus.
source: The pseudo-septation of the apophysis and rhizoids from the cell body is evidence for functional compartmentation (i.e. feeding vs. reproduction) within the thallus of a unicellular fungus.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observation of the pseudo-septum and the different functions of the compartments.

claim: Comparable structures to the apophysis-cell body pseudo-septum are present in other chytrid species.
source: Comparable structures are also present in other chytrid species (e.g. Barr, 1970; Beakes et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barr, 1970; Beakes et al., 1992.

claim: Division of multicellular dikaryan fungi by septa, where continuity between distinct cytoplasmic compartments is maintained by septal pores, is integral to multicellularity, cellular differentiation, and resilience.
source: Division of multicellular dikaryan fungi by septa, where continuity between distinct cytoplasmic compartments is maintained by septal pores, is integral to multicellularity, cellular differentiation, and resilience (Bleichrodt et al., 2015; Bleichrodt et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bleichrodt et al., 2015; Bleichrodt et al., 2012.

claim: The origin of hyphal septa was a major innovation in fungal evolution occurring at the node shared by hyphal and rhizoidal fungi.
source: The origin of hyphal septa was a major innovation in fungal evolution (Berbee et al., 2017; Nagy et al., 2020) occurring at the node shared by hyphal and rhizoidal fungi (Berbee et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Berbee et al., 2017; Nagy et al., 2020.

claim: The role of the apophysis-cell body pseudo-septum in chytrids in delineating functionally dedicated subcellular compartments may represent an evolutionary precursor to dikaryan septa differentiation and multicellularity.
source: The role of the apophysis-cell body pseudo-septum (or an analogous structure) in chytrids in delineating functionally dedicated subcellular compartments may represent an evolutionary precursor to dikaryan septa differentiation and multicellularity.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the functional similarity between the chytrid pseudo-septum and dikaryan septa.

claim: Dikaryan sporogenesis typically involves the septation of hyphal cytoplasm via cell wall synthesis and dikaryan spores are therefore incapable of engulfment activity.
source: Although dikaryan sporogenesis is complex and diverse, it typically involves the septation of hyphal cytoplasm via cell wall synthesis and dikaryan spores are therefore incapable of such engulfment activity (Cole, 1986; Money, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cole, 1986; Money, 2016.

claim: Phagocytosis has not been observed generally in the fungi.
source: Phagocytosis has not been observed generally in the fungi (Yutin et al., 2009), however in representatives of the basal Opisthosporidia, wall-less endoparasites such as Rozella (Cryptomycota) and Aphelidium (Aphelida) have been shown to consume host cytoplasm material via phagocytosis (Powell et al., 2017; Karpov et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yutin et al., 2009; Powell et al., 2017; Karpov et al., 2014.

claim: Wall-less endoparasites such as Rozella (Cryptomycota) and Aphelidium (Aphelida) have been shown to consume host cytoplasm material via phagocytosis.
source: Phagocytosis has not been observed generally in the fungi (Yutin et al., 2009), however in representatives of the basal Opisthosporidia, wall-less endoparasites such as Rozella (Cryptomycota) and Aphelidium (Aphelida) have been shown to consume host cytoplasm material via phagocytosis (Powell et al., 2017; Karpov et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Powell et al., 2017; Karpov et al., 2014.

claim: Nucleariid amoebae, choanoflagellates, and various animal cell types exhibit analogous endocytotic engulfment behaviour as observed in chytrid zoospores.
source: Nucleariid amoebae (Yoshida et al., 2009), choanoflagellates (Laundon et al., 2019), and various animal cell types (Bayne, 1990) also exhibit analogous endocytotic engulfment behaviour as we provide evidence for here in chytrid zoospores.
evidence: Supported by citations to Yoshida et al., 2009; Laundon et al., 2019; Bayne, 1990.

claim: The apparent conservation of engulfment behaviour may indicate that such engulfment behaviour to assimilate subcellular cargo during sporogenesis of wall-less zoospores existed in the last common ancestor of branching fungi and was lost in dikaryan fungi as spores became walled.
source: Chytrid zoosporogenesis warrants further study, however the apparent conservation may indicate that such engulfment behaviour to assimilate subcellular cargo during sporogenesis of wall-less zoospores existed in the last common ancestor of branching fungi and was lost in dikaryan fungi as spores became walled.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observation of engulfment in chytrids and its absence in dikaryan fungi.
